subject: chemistry
title: Electron configuration
summary: Explains the aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule, writing configurations for atoms, ions and the Cr and Cu exceptions, and using effective nuclear charge and Slater's rules to explain periodic trends.
body:
An atom's **electron configuration** is the list of which orbitals its electrons occupy. Configuration explains the layout of the periodic table, the charges ions form, the colours and magnetism of transition metal compounds, and the trends in atomic size and ionisation energy. This lesson sets out the rules for building configurations and then uses effective nuclear charge to explain *why* the periodic trends happen, not just what they are.

## Key ideas

### Orbital energies in many-electron atoms

In hydrogen, all orbitals in the same shell have the same energy. In atoms with more than one electron, electrons repel each other, and subshells within a shell split in energy: **ns < np < nd < nf**. The reason is **penetration**. An s electron has a significant probability of being found very close to the nucleus (inside the inner electrons), so it feels more of the nuclear charge and is lower in energy. A p electron penetrates less and a d electron less again. Because of this, 4s ends up lower in energy than 3d for potassium and calcium, so 4s fills first.

### The three rules for building configurations

1. **Aufbau principle** — electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbitals available first. The usual filling order is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p. This follows the (n + l) rule: lower n + l fills first; if two subshells have equal n + l, the one with lower n fills first.
2. **Pauli exclusion principle** — no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers. So an orbital (fixed n, l, mₗ) holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins (mₛ = +½ and −½).
3. **Hund's rule** — when electrons fill a set of degenerate orbitals (such as the three 2p orbitals), they occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins before any orbital gets a second electron. This minimises electron–electron repulsion, and parallel spins also lower the energy through an effect called exchange energy.

Configurations can be written in full (N: 1s² 2s² 2p³), in **noble gas (condensed) notation** (Fe: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²), or as **orbital box diagrams**, which show the spin arrows and make Hund's rule visible. Electrons in the outermost shell are **valence electrons**; those in the filled inner shells are **core electrons**.

An atom with one or more unpaired electrons is **paramagnetic** (attracted into a magnetic field). An atom with all electrons paired is **diamagnetic** (weakly repelled). Counting unpaired electrons is a common exam task.

### Exceptions: chromium and copper

Two important exceptions in the first transition series are:

- Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (not 3d⁴ 4s²)
- Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (not 3d⁹ 4s²)

The 4s and 3d energies are very close at this point, so the small gain in stability from a half-filled (d⁵) or completely filled (d¹⁰) d subshell, with its reduced repulsion and greater exchange energy, outweighs the cost of moving one electron from 4s to 3d. Similar exceptions occur for Mo and Ag in the period below.

### Configurations of ions

For main group elements, add or remove electrons from the highest-energy subshell: Cl⁻ is [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶, Al³⁺ is [Ne]. Ions and atoms with the same configuration are **isoelectronic** (for example N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺, Mg²⁺).

For transition metals, the **4s electrons are removed before the 3d electrons**, even though 4s filled first. Once the 3d orbitals contain electrons, they drop below 4s in energy, and the 4s electrons, which are further out on average, are the easiest to remove. So Fe ([Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²) forms Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵. Transition metal ions in compounds essentially never have 4s electrons.

### Effective nuclear charge and shielding

An outer electron does not feel the full nuclear charge Z, because inner electrons sit between it and the nucleus and repel it. This is **shielding** (or screening). The net attraction the electron feels is the **effective nuclear charge**:

`Z_eff = Z − S`

where S is the **shielding constant**. A rough estimate is S = number of core electrons. A better estimate uses **Slater's rules**. For an electron in an s or p orbital:

- electrons in the same (ns, np) group each contribute 0.35 (0.30 if the group is 1s);
- electrons in the shell n − 1 each contribute 0.85;
- electrons in shell n − 2 or lower each contribute 1.00;
- electrons in higher shells contribute 0.

(For a d or f electron, every electron in lower groups contributes 1.00.)

### Periodic trends explained with Z_eff

**Across a period** (left to right), Z rises by one each step, but the added electron goes into the same shell, where electrons shield each other poorly (only 0.35 each). So Z_eff on the valence electrons increases steadily. Consequences:

- **Atomic radius decreases**, because the valence electrons are pulled closer.
- **First ionisation energy** (the energy for X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻) **increases**, because valence electrons are held more tightly.
- **Electronegativity increases** for the same reason.

**Down a group**, Z_eff on the valence electrons stays roughly constant (or rises slightly), but n increases, so the valence electrons are in larger orbitals further from the nucleus. So radius increases, and ionisation energy and electronegativity decrease.

**Two dips in first ionisation energy** across period 2 (and period 3) test real understanding:

- **Be > B**: boron's outer electron is in 2p, which penetrates less and is higher in energy than 2s, so it is easier to remove.
- **N > O**: oxygen's fourth 2p electron must pair up in an orbital already holding one electron. The extra repulsion makes it easier to remove, even though Z_eff is higher.

**Successive ionisation energies** rise each time, because each removal leaves an ion of higher positive charge. A very large jump appears when an electron must be taken from a new, inner shell with much higher Z_eff. The position of this jump shows the number of valence electrons.

**Ionic radii**: cations are smaller than their atoms (an outer shell is often lost, and fewer electrons share the same nuclear charge); anions are larger (more electron repulsion for the same Z). In an isoelectronic series, radius decreases as Z increases: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: configurations and unpaired electrons for Co and Co²⁺

Cobalt has Z = 27.

1. Fill in aufbau order: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁷, which is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s².
2. Co²⁺: remove the two 4s electrons first, giving **[Ar] 3d⁷**.
3. Hund's rule for 3d⁷ across five orbitals: put one electron in each of the five (5 electrons), then pair the remaining 2. That leaves 3 orbitals with one electron.
4. Co²⁺ has **3 unpaired electrons** and is paramagnetic.

### Example 2: Slater's rules across period 3

Calculate Z_eff for the valence electron of Na and for a 3p electron of Cl.

Na (Z = 11), grouped (1s²)(2s² 2p⁶)(3s¹):
1. Same group: no other 3s/3p electrons, so 0.
2. n = 2 shell: 8 × 0.85 = 6.80.
3. n = 1 shell: 2 × 1.00 = 2.00.
4. S = 8.80, so Z_eff = 11 − 8.80 = **2.20**.

Cl (Z = 17), grouped (1s²)(2s² 2p⁶)(3s² 3p⁵):
1. Same group: the other 6 electrons in 3s/3p: 6 × 0.35 = 2.10.
2. n = 2: 8 × 0.85 = 6.80. n = 1: 2 × 1.00 = 2.00.
3. S = 10.90, so Z_eff = 17 − 10.90 = **6.10**.

The much larger Z_eff for chlorine explains why Cl is smaller (about 100 pm vs about 186 pm for Na), has a far higher first ionisation energy and is much more electronegative.

### Example 3: Z_eff for the 4s electron of potassium

K (Z = 19): (1s²)(2s² 2p⁶)(3s² 3p⁶)(4s¹). Shell n − 1 = 3 holds 8 electrons: 8 × 0.85 = 6.80. Shells n = 1 and 2 hold 10: 10 × 1.00 = 10.00. S = 16.80, so Z_eff = 19 − 16.80 = **2.20**. This equals Na's value, but the electron is in n = 4, so it is further out and easier to remove. This is why ionisation energy falls down Group 1 even though Z_eff barely changes.

### Example 4: reading successive ionisation energies

An element in period 3 has successive ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹) of 578, 1817, 2745, 11 577 and 14 842. The big jump is between the third and fourth values (about four times larger). So three electrons are removed relatively easily, and the fourth comes from the inner n = 2 shell. The element has 3 valence electrons, so it is in Group 13: **aluminium**.

## Common mistakes

- Removing 3d electrons before 4s when forming transition metal ions. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
- Pairing electrons too early. Hund's rule says fill each degenerate orbital singly first.
- Explaining trends across a period only with "more protons". The key is that Z rises while shielding from same-shell electrons is poor, so Z_eff rises.
- Explaining the N > O dip with "half-filled subshells are stable" alone. The better explanation is the extra repulsion when the fourth p electron pairs.
- Forgetting Cr and Cu exceptions, or applying them to their ions incorrectly (Cu⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰, Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹).

## Exam tips

- For ions, always write the neutral atom first, then remove electrons. This prevents most errors.
- Explanations of trends earn full marks when they mention three factors: nuclear charge (or Z_eff), shielding, and distance (shell number or radius).
- Slater's rules calculations are marked on correct grouping. Write out the grouped configuration before assigning 0.35, 0.85 and 1.00.
- Box diagrams with spin arrows are the clearest way to show unpaired electrons and justify paramagnetism.

## Key terms

- **Electron configuration** — the arrangement of an atom's electrons among its orbitals.
- **Aufbau principle** — electrons fill the lowest-energy available orbitals first.
- **Pauli exclusion principle** — no two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers, so each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins.
- **Hund's rule** — degenerate orbitals are singly occupied, with parallel spins, before pairing begins.
- **Penetration** — the extent to which an electron's probability distribution reaches close to the nucleus, inside inner electrons.
- **Shielding** — the reduction in nuclear attraction felt by an electron due to repulsion from other electrons.
- **Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff)** — the net positive charge experienced by an electron, Z − S.
- **Isoelectronic** — having the same number of electrons and the same configuration.
- **Paramagnetic** — having unpaired electrons and being attracted into a magnetic field.
- **Diamagnetic** — having all electrons paired.
- **First ionisation energy** — the energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms.

## Summary

- In many-electron atoms subshell energies split (ns < np < nd) because of penetration and shielding.
- Configurations follow the aufbau principle, the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund's rule; Cr and Cu are exceptions with 3d⁵ 4s¹ and 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.
- Transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d electrons when they form ions.
- Z_eff = Z − S; Slater's rules give a good estimate of S.
- Z_eff increases across a period, so radius falls and ionisation energy and electronegativity rise; down a group the larger n dominates.
- Dips in ionisation energy (Be > B, N > O) and jumps in successive ionisation energies are explained by subshell energy, electron pairing and shell structure.

questions.prompt: What is the ground-state electron configuration of the Cu²⁺ ion?
questions.explanation: Copper is the exception [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. To form Cu²⁺, first remove the 4s electron, then one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d⁹. Option A comes from removing 3d electrons from the 'expected' 3d⁹ 4s², which is wrong on two counts: Cu is an exception, and 4s electrons are removed first.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Hund's rule?

options.A: No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers.
options.B: Electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before any orbital is doubly occupied.
options.C: Electrons fill orbitals in order of increasing energy.
options.D: An orbital can hold a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins.

questions.explanation: Hund's rule concerns how electrons spread across orbitals of equal energy, which minimises repulsion. Options A and D describe the Pauli exclusion principle (and its consequence), and option C is the aufbau principle.

questions.prompt: How many unpaired electrons are present in a gaseous Mn²⁺ ion (Z = 25)?
questions.explanation: Mn is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s². Removing the two 4s electrons gives Mn²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵. By Hund's rule the five d electrons each occupy a separate orbital, so there are 5 unpaired electrons. Option B (3) results from removing two 3d electrons instead of the 4s electrons, giving 3d³.

questions.prompt: Using Slater's rules, what is the effective nuclear charge felt by a 2p electron in a nitrogen atom (Z = 7)?
questions.explanation: Grouping: (1s²)(2s² 2p³). The other 4 electrons in the n = 2 group each give 0.35 = 1.40; the two 1s electrons are in shell n − 1, each giving 0.85 = 1.70. S = 3.10, so Z_eff = 7 − 3.10 = 3.90. Option A (5.00) uses the crude estimate S = core electrons only, ignoring same-shell shielding.

questions.prompt: The first ionisation energy of oxygen (1314 kJ mol⁻¹) is lower than that of nitrogen (1402 kJ mol⁻¹). Which is the best explanation?

options.A: Oxygen has a smaller nuclear charge than nitrogen.
options.B: Oxygen's outermost electron is in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy than nitrogen's 2s orbital.
options.C: Oxygen's valence electrons are in a higher shell than nitrogen's.
options.D: In oxygen, the electron removed is in a doubly occupied 2p orbital, and electron–electron repulsion in that orbital makes it easier to remove.

questions.explanation: N (2p³) has one electron in each 2p orbital; O (2p⁴) has one pair, and the extra repulsion between the paired electrons raises its energy, so it is removed more easily. Option B is tempting because it is the explanation for the Be > B dip, but both N and O lose a 2p electron.

questions.prompt: Which of the following lists the species in order of DECREASING radius?
questions.explanation: All four ions are isoelectronic with argon (18 electrons). As the nuclear charge increases from S (16) to Ca (20), the same electrons are pulled in more tightly, so radius decreases: S²⁻ > Cl⁻ > K⁺ > Ca²⁺. Option B is the reverse, which follows if you assume more protons means a bigger particle.

questions.prompt: An element in period 3 has successive ionisation energies (kJ mol⁻¹): 738, 1451, 7733, 10 543, 13 630. Which element is it?
questions.explanation: The big jump is between the 2nd (1451) and 3rd (7733) values, so there are 2 valence electrons and the third must come from the inner n = 2 shell. The Group 2 element in period 3 is magnesium. Option B (Al) would show the jump after the third ionisation energy.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why atomic radius decreases from sodium to chlorine across period 3?

options.A: The number of electron shells decreases across the period.
options.B: Electrons added to the same shell shield each other poorly, so the effective nuclear charge on the valence electrons increases.
options.C: Inner-shell electrons shield more effectively as more protons are added.
options.D: Electron–electron repulsion decreases as more electrons are added.

questions.explanation: Z rises by one each step, but each new electron enters the same shell and contributes little shielding (0.35 by Slater's rules), so Z_eff rises (about 2.2 for Na to 6.1 for Cl) and the valence electrons are pulled closer. Option A is wrong because all period 3 atoms have three shells; option C is wrong because the core (1s² 2s² 2p⁶) is the same across the period.
